Real client-certificate verification does exist, at cmd/admin-gateway/main.go:263, where the admin gateway sets ClientAuth: RequireAndVerifyClientCert against a ClientCAs pool loaded from cfg.ClientCAFile at :249 -- but that is a transport gate, not a user assertion: nothing extracts an identity from the peer certificate, and admin identity still comes from the session afterwards, which is what docs/security.md AR-9 records. The trust store itself is assessed under V12.1.3. The previous reason implied that certificate verification happens nowhere, which reads as a stronger statement than the code supports.

requirements.requirement: Verify that the challenge nonce is at least 64 bits in length, and statistically unique or unique over the lifetime of the cryptographic device.
requirements.notes: WebAuthn challenges are 32 CSPRNG bytes. L3 requirement, recorded for completeness.

requirements.requirement: Verify that, if the application supports multiple identity providers (IdPs), the user's identity cannot be spoofed via another supported identity provider (eg. by using the same user identifier). The standard mitigation would be for the application to register and identify the user using a combination of the IdP ID (serving as a namespace) and the user's ID in the IdP.
requirements.notes: Federated identities are keyed on (provider, provider subject), so one provider cannot assert an identity owned by another, and linking requires a verified email.

requirements.requirement: Verify that the presence and integrity of digital signatures on authentication assertions (for example on JWTs or SAML assertions) are always validated, rejecting any assertions that are unsigned or have invalid signatures.
requirements.notes: ID token signatures are verified against the issuer JWKS before any claim is read.

requirements.requirement: Verify that SAML assertions are uniquely processed and used only once within the validity period to prevent replay attacks.
requirements.notes: vault42 implements no SAML. Federation is OAuth 2.0 and OpenID Connect only, so there is no SAML assertion to process or replay.

requirements.requirement: Verify that, if an application uses a separate Identity Provider (IdP) and expects specific authentication strength, methods, or recentness for specific functions, the application verifies this using the information returned by the IdP. For example, if OIDC is used, this might be achieved by validating ID Token claims such as 'acr', 'amr', and 'auth_time' (if present). If the IdP does not provide this information, the application must have a documented fallback approach that assumes that the minimum strength authentication mechanism was used (for example, single-factor authentication using username and password).
requirements.notes: Met on the fallback clause, which is the operative one here. vault42 consumes an upstream identity provider and asks it nothing about how the user was authenticated: no acr, amr or auth_time is read from any ID token. The requirement's final sentence prescribes exactly that case, and internal/handler/oauth.go:649 applies it -- the callback issues through NewAuthContext with MethodFederated as the only method and the user-verification flag clear. AALForMethods treats a provider assertion as a first factor and never as the possession factor that completes AAL2 (internal/service/mfa.go:104), so a federated-only session is stamped at the floor, urn:vault42:aal:1, and emits no amr value because RFC 8176 registers none for an assertion from another issuer. Strength above the floor has to be earned by a factor vault42 verified itself: an MFA-enrolled user still goes through IssueChallengeToken (internal/handler/oauth.go:601), which carries the federated first factor across rather than claiming a password. Previously an accepted risk, CR-21, on the sentence "no acr, amr or aal claim is issued and AALForMethods has no non-test caller"; both halves stopped being true in af780d7 and the row was not moved. What remains true and bounds the claim: vault42 does not verify an upstream acr even when the provider supplies one, which is safe only because the value it substitutes is always the minimum.

requirements.requirement: Verify that the user's session inactivity timeout and absolute maximum session lifetime are documented, are appropriate in combination with other controls, and that the documentation includes justification for any deviations from NIST SP 800-63B re-authentication requirements.
requirements.notes: Met, all three clauses. Both timeouts are documented in docs/config.md and both are configurable: VAULT_MAX_SESSION_LIFETIME (default 720h) and VAULT_INACTIVITY_TIMEOUT (default 1h, internal/config/config.go:574). They are appropriate in combination -- the inactivity window is four access-token lifetimes wide, so a session in normal use never approaches it, and the absolute bound is the outer limit that a rotating client cannot slide. The deviation clause is satisfied and is the reason this row is not simply inherited from the two settings: docs/config.md states the NIST SP 800-63B-4 section 2.2.3 figures (24 hours overall, 1 hour of inactivity), says which one this deployment meets and which it deviates from, and says why. The entry previously cited 12 hours as the AAL2 figure, which is the withdrawn Rev 3 number; a merge reintroduced it after it was first corrected, and TestASVS_V7_1_1_TheDocumentedTimeoutsAreTheEnforcedOnes now fails if it comes back. That test also parses both documented defaults out of the published table and compares them with what config.Load produces, so the document cannot drift from the code in either direction.

requirements.requirement: Verify that the documentation defines how many concurrent (parallel) sessions are allowed for one account as well as the intended behaviors and actions to be taken when the maximum number of active sessions is reached.
requirements.notes: VAULT_MAX_SESSIONS_PER_USER and the 429 too_many_sessions behaviour are documented; AccessTokenTTL and RefreshTokenTTL carry their own documented defaults (internal/config/config.go:88). Note that docs/config.md previously described eviction of the oldest session, which does not happen; correcting that is on the documentation stream.

requirements.requirement: Verify that all systems that create and manage user sessions as part of a federated identity management ecosystem (such as SSO systems) are documented along with controls to coordinate session lifetimes, termination, and any other conditions that require re-authentication.
requirements.notes: The federated login flow and its session boundaries are documented in docs/architecture.md.

requirements.requirement: Verify that the application performs all session token verification using a trusted, backend service.
requirements.notes: Every token is verified server-side against the keystore; nothing is trusted from the client.

requirements.requirement: Verify that the application uses either self-contained or reference tokens that are dynamically generated for session management, i.e. not using static API secrets and keys.
requirements.notes: Sessions are dynamically issued JWT and refresh-token pairs, never static keys.

requirements.requirement: Verify that if reference tokens are used to represent user sessions, they are unique and generated using a cryptographically secure pseudo-random number generator (CSPRNG) and possess at least 128 bits of entropy.
requirements.notes: Refresh tokens are 256 CSPRNG bits.

requirements.requirement: Verify that the application generates a new session token on user authentication, including re-authentication, and terminates the current session token.
requirements.notes: Every authentication and every rotation issues a new token and invalidates the old one first.

requirements.requirement: Verify that there is an inactivity timeout such that re-authentication is enforced according to risk analysis and documented security decisions.
requirements.notes: Met. An inactivity timeout exists, is enforced, and re-authentication is what it requires: a family idle past VAULT_INACTIVITY_TIMEOUT is revoked and refused with ErrSessionIdle, so the way back is a full login rather than another rotation. The mechanism is AuthService.enforceSessionInactivity (internal/service/auth.go:2407), called from the refresh path at internal/service/auth.go:1378 before the presented token is spent. It measures idleness from the presented refresh token's own created_at, which is the instant its family last rotated: a family only advances by rotating, the predecessor row is marked used before the successor is inserted, so the row a client presents is always its family's newest generation. No last_activity_at column was added, because that would be a second copy of a fact the row already carries -- repository.ActiveFamily.LastUsedAt already publishes the same value to the user -- and because stamping activity per request would turn the hottest read path in the service into a write. GetByTokenHash already selects created_at, so the check adds no query and no round trip. The documented security decision the requirement asks for is the default of 1 hour and the reasoning in docs/config.md. The check fails closed on an unreadable issuance instant, the same way the absolute bound fails closed on an unknown family origin.

requirements.requirement: Verify that there is an absolute maximum session lifetime such that re-authentication is enforced according to risk analysis and documented security decisions.
requirements.notes: An absolute maximum session lifetime is enforced from the family's stored creation instant, configured by VAULT_MAX_SESSION_LIFETIME (default 720h) and clamped into every rotated pair. Every branch that cannot date a family refuses rather than passing. The 7-day refresh TTL is no longer a sliding window without a bound. Whether 720h is the right value against the SP 800-63B-4 AAL2 recommendation of 24h is CR-14.

requirements.requirement: Verify that when session termination is triggered (such as logout or expiration), the application disallows any further use of the session. For reference tokens or stateful sessions, this means invalidating the session data at the application backend. Applications using self-contained tokens will need a solution such as maintaining a list of terminated tokens, disallowing tokens produced before a per-user date and time or rotating a per-user signing key.
requirements.notes: Termination revokes the refresh-token family; the access token expires within 15 minutes.

requirements.requirement: Verify that the application terminates all active sessions when a user account is disabled or deleted (such as an employee leaving the company).
requirements.notes: Erasure hard-deletes refresh tokens, and the refresh path re-checks account state on every rotation, so a disabled account cannot extend a session.

requirements.requirement: Verify that the application gives the option to terminate all other active sessions after a successful change or removal of any authentication factor (including password change via reset or recovery and, if present, an MFA settings update).
requirements.notes: Password reset and WebAuthn credential change both revoke all sessions.

requirements.requirement: Verify that all pages that require authentication have easy and visible access to logout functionality.
requirements.notes: Logout is an API endpoint, POST /auth/logout. Whether a page offers easy and visible access to it is decided by the client that renders the page, which is web/src and is assessed separately under the declared scope.

requirements.requirement: Verify that application administrators are able to terminate active sessions for an individual user or for all users.
requirements.notes: Administrators can list and revoke sessions for an individual user through the admin gateway.

requirements.requirement: Verify that the application requires full re-authentication before allowing modifications to sensitive account attributes which may affect authentication such as email address, phone number, MFA configuration, or other information used in account recovery.
requirements.notes: Changes to authentication factors are behind confirmMw, which requires a recent password confirmation.

requirements.requirement: Verify that users are able to view and (having authenticated again with at least one factor) terminate any or all currently active sessions.
requirements.notes: GET /user/sessions lists and DELETE /user/sessions revokes, both behind authentication and fingerprint binding.

requirements.requirement: Verify that session lifetime and termination between Relying Parties (RPs) and Identity Providers (IdPs) behave as documented, requiring re-authentication as necessary such as when the maximum time between IdP authentication events is reached.
requirements.notes:
Accepted as CR-22 for the termination half. The lifetime half moved in 1.0.3: the ID token verifier reads the OIDC auth_time claim and the callback passes it into the AuthContext, so a federated token dates the login to the instant the provider says it authenticated the user rather than to the instant the callback ran. An issuer that asserts none is conformant and falls back to the callback instant, which is the one moment this server can vouch for.

What remains is termination, in both directions: no back-channel logout endpoint exists, so an IdP session ending upstream leaves the vault42 session running until its own deadline, and AuthService.Logout revokes only vault42's tokens, so a vault42 logout leaves the upstream session live.

The row previously named TestASVS_V10_2_1_StateIsIntegrityProtectedAndSessionBound, which asserts the OAuth state parameter is HMAC-signed and session-bound. That is a cross-site-request-forgery gate and would pass whether or not any of this were true, so the row was uncovered. It now names a coupling gate that fails if either half moves without the register moving with it.

requirements.requirement: Verify that creation of a session requires either the user's consent or an explicit action, preventing the creation of new application sessions without user interaction.
requirements.notes: A session is only created by an explicit credential submission or an explicit federated authorization the user initiated, and the state cookie proves the callback belongs to that initiation.

requirements.requirement: Verify that authorization documentation defines rules for restricting function-level and data-specific access based on consumer permissions and resource attributes.
requirements.notes: The permission vocabulary and the role lattice are declared in code and documented.

requirements.requirement: Verify that authorization documentation defines rules for field-level access restrictions (both read and write) based on consumer permissions and resource attributes. Note that these rules might depend on other attribute values of the relevant data object, such as state or status.
requirements.notes: Field-level restrictions are declared on the wire types: the audit fingerprint hash is json:"-" and the admin audit projection selects fields explicitly rather than serialising the model.

requirements.requirement: Verify that the application ensures that function-level access is restricted to consumers with explicit permissions.
requirements.notes: Function-level access is gated per route, and the route table is checked against the permission each route is wired to.

requirements.requirement: Verify that the application ensures that data-specific access is restricted to consumers with explicit permissions to specific data items to mitigate insecure direct object reference (IDOR) and broken object level authorization (BOLA).
requirements.notes: Object access is keyed on a pseudonym derived from the authenticated subject, so there is no caller-supplied object identifier to tamper with; the ciphertext is additionally bound to the owner as AAD, so a row moved between users fails to decrypt. Test repointed in the register-integrity pass to a case that exercises the clause directly.

requirements.requirement: Verify that the application ensures that field-level access is restricted to consumers with explicit permissions to specific fields to mitigate broken object property level authorization (BOPLA).
requirements.notes: Responses are built from explicit view types rather than serialised models. internal/adminapi/handler.go:193 declares userSummary, the type both admin user reads project onto, so a field added to model.User does not reach a response by default.

requirements.requirement: Verify that the application enforces authorization rules at a trusted service layer and doesn't rely on controls that an untrusted consumer could manipulate, such as client-side JavaScript.
requirements.notes: Authorization is enforced in middleware on the server; nothing is delegated to the client.

requirements.requirement: Verify that multi-tenant applications use cross-tenant controls to ensure consumer operations will never affect tenants with which they do not have permissions to interact.
requirements.notes: Tenancy is the client_id axis on service documents and the per-subject pseudonym on identity and blobs; both are applied in the query, not after it. Every ServiceDocumentRepo read carries client_id in its WHERE clause (internal/repository/postgres/servicedoc.go:142), so a document belonging to another client is not fetched and then filtered, it is never selected.

requirements.requirement: Verify that self-contained tokens are validated using their digital signature or MAC to protect against tampering before accepting the token's contents.
requirements.notes: Signature verification precedes any use of claim content, and the token is size-bounded before parsing.

requirements.requirement: Verify that only algorithms on an allowlist can be used to create and verify self-contained tokens, for a given context. The allowlist must include the permitted algorithms, ideally only either symmetric or asymmetric algorithms, and must not include the 'None' algorithm. If both symmetric and asymmetric must be supported, additional controls will be needed to prevent key confusion.
requirements.notes: RS256 only. The verifier has no symmetric or none branch at all, so key confusion is structurally impossible.

requirements.requirement: Verify that key material that is used to validate self-contained tokens is from trusted pre-configured sources for the token issuer, preventing attackers from specifying untrusted sources and keys. For JWTs and other JWS structures, headers such as 'jku', 'x5u', and 'jwk' must be validated against an allowlist of trusted sources.
requirements.notes: jku, x5u, x5c and jwk are rejected outright rather than allowlisted, and kid is constrained to a hex pattern.

requirements.requirement: Verify that, if a validity time span is present in the token data, the token and its content are accepted only if the verification time is within this validity time span. For example, for JWTs, the claims 'nbf' and 'exp' must be verified.
requirements.notes: exp is required, nbf and iat are checked when present.

requirements.requirement: Verify that the service receiving a token validates the token to be the correct type and is meant for the intended purpose before accepting the token's contents. For example, only access tokens can be accepted for authorization decisions and only ID Tokens can be used for proving user authentication.
requirements.notes: Access tokens and ID tokens are parsed by separate code paths with separate key sets and separate expected issuers, so neither can be presented in the other's place.

requirements.requirement: Verify that the service only accepts tokens which are intended for use with that service (audience). For JWTs, this can be achieved by validating the 'aud' claim against an allowlist defined in the service.
requirements.notes: The aud claim is validated against the configured value.

requirements.requirement: Verify that, if a token issuer uses the same private key for issuing tokens to different audiences, the issued tokens contain an audience restriction that uniquely identifies the intended audiences. This will prevent a token from being reused with an unintended audience. If the audience identifier is dynamically provisioned, the token issuer must validate these audiences in order to make sure that they do not result in audience impersonation.
requirements.notes: Audience is the configured issuer identity and is not caller-provisioned, so audience impersonation has no input to work with.

requirements.requirement: Verify that tokens are only sent to components that strictly need them. For example, when using a backend-for-frontend pattern for browser-based JavaScript applications, access and refresh tokens shall only be accessible for the backend.
requirements.notes: The refresh token is delivered as a __Host- HttpOnly cookie, never to page JavaScript.

requirements.requirement: Verify that the client only accepts values from the authorization server (such as the authorization code or ID Token) if these values result from an authorization flow that was initiated by the same user agent session and transaction. This requires that client-generated secrets, such as the proof key for code exchange (PKCE) 'code_verifier', 'state' or OIDC 'nonce', are not guessable, are specific to the transaction, and are securely bound to both the client and the user agent session in which the transaction was started.
requirements.notes: The callback is accepted only when the state HMAC verifies and the mirrored __Host- cookie hash matches, which binds it to the user agent session that started the flow.

requirements.requirement: Verify that, if the code flow is used, the OAuth client has protection against browser-based request forgery attacks, commonly known as cross-site request forgery (CSRF), which trigger token requests, either by using proof key for code exchange (PKCE) functionality or checking the 'state' parameter that was sent in the authorization request.
requirements.notes: HMAC-signed state plus a host-only mirrored cookie.

requirements.requirement: Verify that, if the OAuth client can interact with more than one authorization server, it has a defense against mix-up attacks. For example, it could require that the authorization server return the 'iss' parameter value and validate it in the authorization response and the token response.
requirements.notes: The state payload names the provider it was minted for and the callback rejects a mismatch, which is the mix-up defence.

requirements.requirement: Verify that the resource server only accepts access tokens that are intended for use with that service (audience). The audience may be included in a structured access token (such as the 'aud' claim in JWT), or it can be checked using the token introspection endpoint.
requirements.notes: Audience is validated on every access token.

requirements.requirement: Verify that the resource server enforces authorization decisions based on claims from the access token that define delegated authorization. If claims such as 'sub', 'scope', and 'authorization_details' are present, they must be part of the decision.
requirements.notes: Scopes are parsed from the access token and matched exactly, with no prefix matching in either direction.

requirements.requirement: Verify that if an access control decision requires identifying a unique user from an access token (JWT or related token introspection response), the resource server identifies the user from claims that cannot be reassigned to other users. Typically, it means using a combination of 'iss' and 'sub' claims.
requirements.notes: The subject is an immutable UUID that is never reassigned, not an email or username.

requirements.requirement: Verify that, if the resource server requires specific authentication strength, methods, or recentness, it verifies that the presented access token satisfies these constraints. For example, if present, using the OIDC 'acr', 'amr' and 'auth_time' claims respectively.
requirements.notes: Met. vault42 is the resource server for its own access tokens, and it does require authentication recentness for specific functions: the destructive account operations sit behind middleware.Confirmed, which refuses unless POST /auth/confirm re-verified the password within the last five minutes. The constraint is checked against the presented token rather than against session state -- the confirmation record holds the jti of the access token that performed it, and internal/middleware/auth.go:267 refuses any other one -- so a confirmation cannot be carried across a rotation. That is a tighter binding than the auth_time comparison the requirement offers as its example, which survives rotation and is asserted by the issuer rather than checked. The guarded routes are DELETE /user/identity (internal/server/server.go:686) and both blob deletes. No route requires a specific authentication strength or method, so those two limbs have no antecedent; strength is nevertheless expressible from the token alone, because VaultClaims now carries acr, amr and auth_time (internal/crypto/jwt.go:47) populated from the observed authentication event, which is how a downstream resource server would apply the same constraint. Previously an accepted risk, CR-21, on the claim that no acr, amr or aal claim is issued.

requirements.requirement: Verify that the authorization server validates redirect URIs based on a client-specific allowlist of pre-registered URIs using exact string comparison.
requirements.notes: This requirement addresses an authorization server acting for third-party clients. In the OAuth flows vault42 takes part in, it is the client: GET /auth/oauth2/authorize redirects to an upstream provider chosen from a static map, and the post-login redirect target is the server's own configured origin. Neither is a caller-supplied redirect_uri, so the allowlist this requirement asks the authorization server to keep has nothing to match against. Registered client redirect URIs are stored for operator record-keeping. TestASVS_V3_7_2_EveryRedirectTargetIsServerControlled asserts the redirect property that makes this true.

requirements.requirement: Verify that, if the authorization server returns the authorization code in the authorization response, it can be used only once for a token request. For the second valid request with an authorization code that has already been used to issue an access token, the authorization server must reject a token request and revoke any issued tokens related to the authorization code.
requirements.notes: The exchange code is consumed with an atomic get-and-delete, so a second presentation finds nothing.

requirements.requirement: Verify that the authorization code is short-lived. The maximum lifetime can be up to 10 minutes for L1 and L2 applications and up to 1 minute for L3 applications.
requirements.notes: The exchange code TTL is well inside the 10-minute ceiling.

requirements.requirement: Verify that for a given client, the authorization server only allows the usage of grants that this client needs to use. Note that the grants 'token' (Implicit flow) and 'password' (Resource Owner Password Credentials flow) must no longer be used.
requirements.notes: Only the client-credentials grant and vault42's own login flow exist. There is no implicit flow and no resource-owner password grant endpoint.

requirements.requirement: Verify that the authorization server mitigates refresh token replay attacks for public clients, preferably using sender-constrained refresh tokens, i.e., Demonstrating Proof of Possession (DPoP) or Certificate-Bound Access Tokens using mutual TLS (mTLS). For L1 and L2 applications, refresh token rotation may be used. If refresh token rotation is used, the authorization server must invalidate the refresh token after usage, and revoke all refresh tokens for that authorization if an already used and invalidated refresh token is provided.
requirements.notes: ASVS L1 permits rotation in place of sender-constrained refresh credentials. Login starts a family; AuthService.Refresh invalidates the presented value before minting the next (compare-and-set plus family revoke on reuse). DPoP stamps cnf.jkt on access and challenge credentials only. Refresh credentials stay unbound. Rotation is the claim here.

requirements.requirement: Verify that, if the code grant is used, the authorization server mitigates authorization code interception attacks by requiring proof key for code exchange (PKCE). For authorization requests, the authorization server must require a valid 'code_challenge' value and must not accept a 'code_challenge_method' value of 'plain'. For a token request, it must require validation of the 'code_verifier' parameter.
requirements.notes: S256 on every provider: the challenge is SHA256Base64URL over a 32-byte verifier (internal/handler/oauth.go:83), and plain is never offered.

requirements.requirement: Verify that if the authorization server supports unauthenticated dynamic client registration, it mitigates the risk of malicious client applications. It must validate client metadata such as any registered URIs, ensure the user's consent, and warn the user before processing an authorization request with an untrusted client application.
requirements.notes: vault42 supports no dynamic client registration. Clients are provisioned by an operator through the admin gateway.

requirements.requirement: Verify that refresh tokens have an absolute expiration, including if sliding refresh token expiration is applied.
requirements.notes: Met: sliding refresh expiration is bounded by an absolute family deadline, which is exactly the case this requirement calls out. Migration 013 stores the family origin (family_created_at, NOT NULL with a default) so the deadline cannot be reset by rotation or by pruning a spent row; TokenService clamps a rotated pair to origin plus the configured maximum and AuthService.enforceSessionLifetime refuses a family past it; cmd/vault/main.go:414 configures the bound. The test that used to back this row could never fail: it searched migrations/001_initial_schema.sql for a column that landed in 013_session_lifetime.sql. Its replacement reads every migration.

requirements.requirement: Verify that refresh tokens and reference access tokens can be revoked by an authorized user using the authorization server user interface, to mitigate the risk of malicious clients or stolen tokens.
requirements.notes: DELETE /user/sessions revokes every family for the authenticated user.

requirements.requirement: Verify that confidential client is authenticated for client-to-authorized server backchannel requests such as token requests, pushed authorization requests (PAR), and token revocation requests.
requirements.notes: The client-credentials token request authenticates the client by secret over HTTP Basic or the request body.

requirements.requirement: Verify that the authorization server configuration only assigns the required scopes to the OAuth client.
requirements.notes: Issued scopes are the intersection of the request and the client's registered set, so a client cannot obtain a scope it was not granted.

requirements.requirement: Verify that the client (as the relying party) mitigates ID Token replay attacks. For example, by ensuring that the 'nonce' claim in the ID Token matches the 'nonce' value sent in the authentication request to the OpenID Provider (in OAuth2 refereed to as the authorization request sent to the authorization server).
requirements.notes: The nonce is bound and an absent expected nonce fails closed rather than skipping the check.

requirements.requirement: Verify that the client uniquely identifies the user from ID Token claims, usually the 'sub' claim, which cannot be reassigned to other users (for the scope of an identity provider).
requirements.notes: Federated users are keyed on the provider subject, which the provider does not reassign.

requirements.requirement: Verify that the client rejects attempts by a malicious authorization server to impersonate another authorization server through authorization server metadata. The client must reject authorization server metadata if the issuer URL in the authorization server metadata does not exactly match the pre-configured issuer URL expected by the client.
requirements.notes: The discovery document's issuer must equal the configured issuer.

requirements.requirement: Verify that the client validates that the ID Token is intended to be used for that client (audience) by checking that the 'aud' claim from the token is equal to the 'client_id' value for the client.
requirements.notes: aud is checked against the client id.

requirements.requirement: Verify that, when using OIDC back-channel logout, the relying party mitigates denial of service through forced logout and cross-JWT confusion in the logout flow. The client must verify that the logout token is correctly typed with a value of 'logout+jwt', contains the 'event' claim with the correct member name, and does not contain a 'nonce' claim. Note that it is also recommended to have a short expiration (e.g., 2 minutes).
requirements.notes: vault42 implements no OIDC back-channel logout.

requirements.requirement: Verify that the OpenID Provider only allows values 'code', 'ciba', 'id_token', or 'id_token code' for response mode. Note that 'code' is preferred over 'id_token code' (the OIDC Hybrid flow), and 'token' (any Implicit flow) must not be used.
requirements.notes: This requirement constrains the response types an OpenID Provider offers. vault42 occupies the relying party role, not the provider role: it publishes a deliberately minimal discovery document carrying its issuer, JWKS URI and access-token signing algorithm, and internal/handler/wellknown.go:71 explains in a comment which fields are omitted and why, rather than faking them. Response types are chosen at an authorization endpoint, and vault42 acts as a client at the one it uses, which belongs to the upstream provider. TestASVS_AbsentEndpointsAreActuallyAbsent asserts the discovery document advertises nothing it does not implement.

requirements.requirement: Verify that the OpenID Provider mitigates denial of service through forced logout. By obtaining explicit confirmation from the end-user or, if present, validating parameters in the logout request (initiated by the relying party), such as the 'id_token_hint'.
requirements.notes: vault42 is not an OpenID Provider and offers no RP-initiated logout endpoint.

requirements.requirement: Verify that the authorization server ensures that the user consents to each authorization request. If the identity of the client cannot be assured, the authorization server must always explicitly prompt the user for consent.
requirements.notes: This requirement addresses an authorization server mediating delegation to a third party. vault42's clients are first-party and operator-provisioned through the admin plane, so the end user is never asked to delegate access to a party the operator did not install. Consent for data processing, which is a different question, is covered by the GDPR Art. 6 and Art. 7 rows.

requirements.requirement: Verify that when the authorization server prompts for user consent, it presents sufficient and clear information about what is being consented to. When applicable, this should include the nature of the requested authorizations (typically based on scope, resource server, Rich Authorization Requests (RAR) authorization details), the identity of the authorized application, and the lifetime of these authorizations.
requirements.notes: V10.7.1 places the consent prompt outside vault42's role: clients are first-party and operator-provisioned, so there is no third-party delegation to prompt for and no consent screen whose content this requirement would constrain. TestASVS_AbsentEndpointsAreActuallyAbsent asserts the route table carries no consent endpoint.

requirements.requirement: Verify that the user can review, modify, and revoke consents which the user has granted through the authorization server.
requirements.notes: The reviewable and revocable grants that do exist are federated identity links (DELETE /user/social/{id}), marketing consent and active sessions, each with its own endpoint.

requirements.requirement: Verify that there is a documented policy for management of cryptographic keys and a cryptographic key lifecycle that follows a key management standard such as NIST SP 800-57. This should include ensuring that keys are not overshared (for example, with more than two entities for shared secrets and more than one entity for private keys).
requirements.notes: The key lifecycle (active, retired, revoked) and its management are documented, and private keys are held by one entity.

requirements.requirement: Verify that a cryptographic inventory is performed, maintained, regularly updated, and includes all cryptographic keys, algorithms, and certificates used by the application. It must also document where keys can and cannot be used in the system, and the types of data that can and cannot be protected using the keys.
requirements.notes: The cryptographic inventory (AES-256-GCM, Argon2id, HMAC-SHA256, RS256, HKDF) is documented and pinned by test.

requirements.requirement: Verify that industry-validated implementations (including libraries and hardware-accelerated implementations) are used for cryptographic operations.
requirements.notes: Go standard library and golang.org/x/crypto only; no hand-rolled primitive.

requirements.requirement: Verify that the application is designed with crypto agility such that random number, authenticated encryption, MAC, or hashing algorithms, key lengths, rounds, ciphers and modes can be reconfigured, upgraded, or swapped at any time, to protect against cryptographic breaks. Similarly, it must also be possible to replace keys and passwords and re-encrypt data. This will allow for seamless upgrades to post-quantum cryptography (PQC), once high-assurance implementations of approved PQC schemes or standards are widely available.
requirements.notes: Keys rotate through a versioned keystore with kid selection, and the algorithm is a single named constant, so a swap is one edit plus a rotation rather than a data migration.

requirements.requirement: Verify that all cryptographic primitives utilize a minimum of 128-bits of security based on the algorithm, key size, and configuration. For example, a 256-bit ECC key provides roughly 128 bits of security where RSA requires a 3072-bit key to achieve 128 bits of security.
requirements.notes: AES-256 and RSA-2048 minimum. RSA-2048 provides about 112 bits rather than 128; it is the interoperability floor for JWT verification and the JWKS advertises the key size, so a consumer can apply its own policy.

requirements.requirement: Verify that insecure block modes (e.g., ECB) and weak padding schemes (e.g., PKCS#1 v1.5) are not used.
requirements.notes: GCM only. No ECB, no CBC, no PKCS#1 v1.5.

requirements.requirement: Verify that only approved ciphers and modes such as AES with GCM are used.
requirements.notes: AES-256-GCM.

requirements.requirement: Verify that encrypted data is protected against unauthorized modification preferably by using an approved authenticated encryption method or by combining an approved encryption method with an approved MAC algorithm.
requirements.notes: AEAD: tampering and truncation both fail the open.

requirements.requirement: Verify that only approved hash functions are used for general cryptographic use cases, including digital signatures, HMAC, KDF, and random bit generation. Disallowed hash functions, such as MD5, must not be used for any cryptographic purpose.
requirements.notes: SHA-256 throughout. SHA-1 appears in exactly two protocol-mandated places, TOTP (RFC 6238) and the HIBP k-anonymity range API, both annotated at the import and neither used for a security decision. MD5 has zero occurrences repo-wide.

requirements.requirement: Verify that passwords are stored using an approved, computationally intensive, key derivation function (also known as a "password hashing function"), with parameter settings configured based on current guidance. The settings should balance security and performance to make brute-force attacks sufficiently challenging for the required level of security.
requirements.notes: Argon2id at 46 MiB, 1 iteration, 1 lane, with a 16-byte salt and a server-side pepper.

requirements.requirement: Verify that hash functions used in digital signatures, as part of data authentication or data integrity are collision resistant and have appropriate bit-lengths. If collision resistance is required, the output length must be at least 256 bits. If only resistance to second pre-image attacks is required, the output length must be at least 128 bits.
requirements.notes: SHA-256, 256-bit output.

requirements.requirement: Verify that the application uses approved key derivation functions with key stretching parameters when deriving secret keys from passwords. The parameters in use must balance security and performance to prevent brute-force attacks from compromising the resulting cryptographic key.
requirements.notes: HKDF-SHA256 with domain separation for KEK derivation; Argon2id where the input is a password.

requirements.requirement: Verify that all random numbers and strings which are intended to be non-guessable must be generated using a cryptographically secure pseudo-random number generator (CSPRNG) and have at least 128 bits of entropy. Note that UUIDs do not respect this condition.
requirements.notes: crypto/rand everywhere. math/rand is not imported in any security path.

requirements.requirement: Verify that only approved cryptographic algorithms and modes of operation are used for key generation and seeding, and digital signature generation and verification. Key generation algorithms must not generate insecure keys vulnerable to known attacks, for example, RSA keys which are vulnerable to Fermat factorization.
requirements.notes: Keys are generated by crypto/rsa with the standard library's primality checks.

requirements.requirement: Verify that only the latest recommended versions of the TLS protocol are enabled, such as TLS 1.2 and TLS 1.3. The latest version of the TLS protocol must be the preferred option.
requirements.notes: Inbound listeners are TLS 1.3: the HTTP server sets MinVersion: tls.VersionTLS13 (internal/server/server.go:224). The Redis client floor is TLS 1.2, which this requirement permits; it is lower because the peer’s capability is the operator’s, not vault42’s.

requirements.requirement: Verify that only recommended cipher suites are enabled, with the strongest cipher suites set as preferred. L3 applications must only support cipher suites which provide forward secrecy.
requirements.notes: TLS 1.3 offers only forward-secret AEAD suites, so the cipher-suite requirement is satisfied by the version pin.

requirements.requirement: Verify that the application validates that mTLS client certificates are trusted before using the certificate identity for authentication or authorization.
requirements.notes: RequireAndVerifyClientCert against a configured CA pool.

requirements.requirement: Verify that TLS is used for all connectivity between a client and external facing, HTTP-based services, and does not fall back to insecure or unencrypted communications.
requirements.notes: The non-dev profile refuses to start without TLS unless an explicit override is set.

requirements.requirement: Verify that external facing services use publicly trusted TLS certificates.
requirements.notes: Certificates are supplied by the operator; the deployment guide requires publicly trusted certificates for the external origin.

requirements.requirement: Verify that an encrypted protocol such as TLS is used for all inbound and outbound connections to and from the application, including monitoring systems, management tools, remote access and SSH, middleware, databases, mainframes, partner systems, or external APIs. The server must not fall back to insecure or unencrypted protocols.
requirements.notes: Accepted risk CR-34. The outbound-mail half closed: internal/email/smtp.go:111 replaced net/smtp.SendMail with an explicit conversation that upgrades when the relay advertises STARTTLS, returns ErrSMTPNoSTARTTLS when it does not, and pins tls.VersionTLS12; the opt-out is accepted outside dev only for a loopback SMTP host. Every other outbound destination is encrypted by construction: SendGrid, the HIBP range API and the three social providers are hardcoded https, and fetchableEndpoint refuses an OIDC issuer or any endpoint its discovery document names unless it is https or loopback http. Inbound listeners pin TLS 1.3 and Postgres defaults to sslmode=require, refusing disable, allow and prefer without an explicit override. What is left is the Redis link. The dial path can negotiate TLS (internal/redis/pool.go:184), but internal/cache/redis.go:19 builds the Options without it and no configuration key sets it, so the cache connection is cleartext and an operator has no way to change that. It carries the Redis AUTH password, rate-limit and lockout keys bearing client IP addresses and user identifiers, and the jti that binds a password-confirmation window; the email one-time code is not exposed, because it is stored as an HMAC. The previous reason on this row described opportunistic STARTTLS, which has not been the behaviour since d530d6c.

requirements.requirement: Verify that TLS clients validate certificates received before communicating with a TLS server.
requirements.notes: No shipped code sets InsecureSkipVerify, enforced structurally over the whole tree.

requirements.requirement: Verify that TLS or another appropriate transport encryption mechanism used for all connectivity between internal, HTTP-based services within the application, and does not fall back to insecure or unencrypted communications.
requirements.notes: Redis TLS is available, and the Postgres DSN defaults to DBSSLMode "require" (internal/config/config.go:498). A profile configuring an SSL mode outside the encrypted set logs a security warning naming what travels in cleartext. Dev substitutes sslmode=disable deliberately, against a loopback database.

requirements.requirement: Verify that TLS connections between internal services use trusted certificates. Where internally generated or self-signed certificates are used, the consuming service must be configured to only trust specific internal CAs and specific self-signed certificates.
requirements.notes: Internal TLS clients validate against the system or operator-supplied trust store; verification is never skipped.

requirements.requirement: Verify that all communication needs for the application are documented. This must include external services which the application relies upon and cases where an end user might be able to provide an external location to which the application will then connect.
requirements.notes: External dependencies (Postgres, Redis, SMTP or SendGrid, OIDC providers) are documented.

requirements.requirement: Verify that communications between backend application components that don't support the application's standard user session mechanism, including APIs, middleware, and data layers, are authenticated. Authentication must use individual service accounts, short-term tokens, or certificate-based authentication and not unchanging credentials such as passwords, API keys, or shared accounts with privileged access.
requirements.notes: Separate database roles (vault_mig, vault_app, vault_admin) with separate credentials, supplied per role.

requirements.requirement: Verify that communications between backend application components, including local or operating system services, APIs, middleware, and data layers, are performed with accounts assigned the least necessary privileges.
requirements.notes: vault_app holds SELECT and INSERT on the audit table and nothing more; migration 002 narrows it further.

requirements.requirement: Verify that if a credential has to be used for service authentication, the credential being used by the consumer is not a default credential (e.g., root/root or admin/admin).
requirements.notes: Every secret is loaded from a file path through config.LoadSecret (internal/config/secrets.go:18), which reads the path named by a _FILE variable and has no default to fall back to: an unset variable is an error at startup, not a built-in credential.

requirements.requirement: Verify that an allowlist is used to define the external resources or systems with which the application is permitted to communicate (e.g., for outbound requests, data loads, or file access). This allowlist can be implemented at the application layer, web server, firewall, or a combination of different layers.
requirements.notes: The chart ships a 259-line NetworkPolicy, enabled by default (charts/vault/values.yaml:380, networkPolicy.enabled), restricting egress to Postgres, Redis, DNS and SMTP.

requirements.requirement: Verify that the web or application server is configured with an allowlist of resources or systems to which the server can send requests or load data or files from.
requirements.notes: Outbound destinations are the configured issuer, mail relay and cache; the NetworkPolicy enforces the same set at the network layer.

requirements.requirement: Verify that a secrets management solution, such as a key vault, is used to securely create, store, control access to, and destroy backend secrets. These could include passwords, key material, integrations with databases and third-party systems, keys and seeds for time-based tokens, other internal secrets, and API keys. Secrets must not be included in application source code or included in build artifacts. For an L3 application, this must involve a hardware-backed solution such as an HSM.
requirements.notes: Secrets are read from files supplied by the platform secret store, never from source or build artifacts, and byte-typed key material is zeroed on shutdown.

requirements.requirement: Verify that access to secret assets adheres to the principle of least privilege.
requirements.notes: Each process reads only the secrets its role needs; the migration password is not read by the application role.

requirements.requirement: Verify that the application is deployed either without any source control metadata, including the .git or .svn folders, or in a way that these folders are inaccessible both externally and to the application itself.
requirements.notes: The image is built from a scratch-style final stage containing the binary and its static assets only. Test repointed in the register-integrity pass to a case that exercises the clause directly.

requirements.requirement: Verify that debug modes are disabled for all components in production environments to prevent exposure of debugging features and information leakage.
requirements.notes: The default profile is production and an unrecognised profile falls through to production; the dev relaxations are reachable only by naming the dev profile explicitly. applyProfileDefaults is where the profile decides the defaults: the dev relaxations are reachable only by naming the dev profile, and anything unrecognised falls through to the production settings.

requirements.requirement: Verify that web servers do not expose directory listings to clients unless explicitly intended.
requirements.notes: The static handler serves the SPA entry point and named assets; it produces no directory index.

requirements.requirement: Verify that using the HTTP TRACE method is not supported in production environments, to avoid potential information leakage.
requirements.notes: Go's ServeMux routes by method pattern: every route this server registers names its method (http.NewServeMux at internal/server/server.go:373, routes from :515), so TRACE matches no pattern and the mux answers 405 without any application code having to enumerate the methods it refuses.

requirements.requirement: Verify that documentation (such as for internal APIs) and monitoring endpoints are not exposed unless explicitly intended.
requirements.notes: The metrics collector is mounted only when explicitly enabled, and no longer on the public listener at all: it has its own http.Server on its own port with its own mux and timeouts (internal/server/server.go:306 and :327), so a scrape target is not reachable through the API surface and cannot inherit its middleware or its exposure. The admin plane remains a separate binary on loopback behind mutual TLS.

requirements.requirement: Verify that all sensitive data created and processed by the application has been identified and classified into protection levels. This includes data that is only encoded and therefore easily decoded, such as Base64 strings or the plaintext payload inside a JWT. Protection levels need to take into account any data protection and privacy regulations and standards which the application is required to comply with.
requirements.notes: The inventory and its protection levels are documented, and the scrub lists are the executable half.

requirements.requirement: Verify that all sensitive data protection levels have a documented set of protection requirements. This must include (but not be limited to) requirements related to general encryption, integrity verification, retention, how the data is to be logged, access controls around sensitive data in logs, database-level encryption, privacy and privacy-enhancing technologies to be used, and other confidentiality requirements.
requirements.notes: Encryption, retention, logging and access rules are stated per data class.

requirements.requirement: Verify that sensitive data is only sent to the server in the HTTP message body or header fields, and that the URL and query string do not contain sensitive information, such as an API key or session token.
requirements.notes: No credential appears in any route pattern or query string. The OAuth callback carries a single-use exchange code in the URL fragment (internal/handler/oauth.go:753), which browsers do not send to the server and no proxy or access log records; the access token itself is never in the redirect at all, it is held in the cache under the hash of that code and collected by POST /auth/oauth2/exchange.

requirements.requirement: Verify that the application prevents sensitive data from being cached in server components, such as load balancers and application caches, or ensures that the data is securely purged after use.
requirements.notes: Single-use artifacts are purged atomically as they are read; no plaintext PII is cached.

requirements.requirement: Verify that defined sensitive data is not sent to untrusted parties (e.g., user trackers) to prevent unwanted collection of data outside of the application's control.
requirements.notes: No analytics, tracker or third-party beacon exists. Addresses are pseudonymised before logging by httputil.ObfuscatedIP (internal/httputil/safelog.go:44), which zeroes the last octet of an IPv4 address and the lower 64 bits of an IPv6 one.

requirements.requirement: Verify that controls around sensitive data related to encryption, integrity verification, retention, how the data is to be logged, access controls around sensitive data in logs, privacy and privacy-enhancing technologies, are implemented as defined in the documentation for the specific data's protection level.
requirements.notes: Scrubbing, retention and access control are implemented as documented for each class. Retention.Sweep (internal/audit/retention.go:141) is the mechanised half, and migration 032 batches it so a long horizon does not lock the table.

requirements.requirement: Verify that authenticated data is cleared from client storage, such as the browser DOM, after the client or session is terminated. The 'Clear-Site-Data' HTTP response header field may be able to help with this but the client-side should also be able to clear up if the server connection is not available when the session is terminated.
requirements.notes: Clearing authenticated data from client storage is a property of the browser application, which the declared scope assesses separately. The half the server owns is done: the session cookie is expired with MaxAge -1 on logout (clearRefreshCookie, internal/handler/auth.go:434) and the refresh family is revoked server-side, so a client that fails to clear its own storage still holds nothing that authenticates.

requirements.requirement: Verify that the application sets sufficient anti-caching HTTP response header fields (i.e., Cache-Control: no-store) so that sensitive data is not cached in browsers.
requirements.notes: Cache-Control: no-store and Pragma: no-cache on every API response; only the public metadata documents opt into caching.

requirements.requirement: Verify that data stored in browser storage (such as localStorage, sessionStorage, IndexedDB, or cookies) does not contain sensitive data, with the exception of session tokens.
requirements.notes: The only value vault42 places in browser storage is the session token itself, as a __Host- HttpOnly cookie, which is the exception this requirement allows.

requirements.requirement: Verify that application documentation defines risk based remediation time frames for 3rd party component versions with vulnerabilities and for updating libraries in general, to minimize the risk from these components.
evidence: .github/workflows/nightly-security.yml#introduce a HIGH CVE that only surfaces on main at 03:00 the next day.
requirements.notes: SECURITY.md states the remediation windows; the nightly scan is the detection mechanism.

requirements.requirement: Verify that an inventory catalog, such as software bill of materials (SBOM), is maintained of all third-party libraries in use, including verifying that components come from pre-defined, trusted, and continually maintained repositories.
evidence: .github/workflows/release.yml#reading is done. Jobs that have to treat a candidate differently,
requirements.notes: An SBOM is attached to every released image, with build provenance and a cosign signature.

requirements.requirement: Verify that the application documentation identifies functionality which is time-consuming or resource-demanding. This must include how to prevent a loss of availability due to overusing this functionality and how to avoid a situation where building a response takes longer than the consumer's timeout. Potential defenses may include asynchronous processing, using queues, and limiting parallel processes per user and per application.
requirements.notes: Argon2id is the deliberately expensive operation and is documented with its concurrency semaphore.

requirements.requirement: Verify that the application only contains components which have not breached the documented update and remediation time frames.
requirements.notes: Transitive floors are declared as pnpm overrides and asserted against the lockfile; the Go toolchain is pinned.

requirements.requirement: Verify that the application has implemented defenses against loss of availability due to functionality which is time-consuming or resource-demanding, based on the documented security decisions and strategies for this.
requirements.notes: The Argon2id semaphore sheds load with 503 rather than exhausting memory, and request bodies are capped at 8 KiB.

requirements.requirement: Verify that the production environment only includes functionality that is required for the application to function, and does not expose extraneous functionality such as test code, sample snippets, and development functionality.
requirements.notes: Optional surfaces are each mounted only when configured: the embedded frontend behind cfg.ServeFrontend (internal/server/server.go:889), metrics on its own listener, and the OAuth, registration, blob and KMS routes each behind their own switch. A surface that is not mounted is not attack surface.

requirements.requirement: Verify that the application only returns the required subset of fields from a data object. For example, it should not return an entire data object, as some individual fields should not be accessible to users.
requirements.notes: Responses are explicit view types. The audit fingerprint hash is json:"-" so it cannot leak through a model serialisation.

requirements.requirement: Verify that where the application backend makes calls to external URLs, it is configured to not follow redirects unless it is intended functionality.
requirements.notes: Outbound provider calls target the pinned issuer; the discovery document's issuer is verified rather than followed.

requirements.requirement: Verify that the application has countermeasures to protect against mass assignment attacks by limiting allowed fields per controller and action, e.g., it is not possible to insert or update a field value when it was not intended to be part of that action.
requirements.notes: DisallowUnknownFields on the public API rejects a request carrying a field the handler did not declare, which is the mass-assignment vector. The admin plane decodes without it, which is a lower-severity gap noted for the handoff since the plane is loopback-only behind mutual TLS.

requirements.requirement: Verify that all proxying and middleware components transfer the user's original IP address correctly using trusted data fields that cannot be manipulated by the end user, and the application and web server use this correct value for logging and security decisions such as rate limiting, taking into account that even the original IP address may not be reliable due to dynamic IPs, VPNs, or corporate firewalls.
requirements.notes: The client address is taken from the connection unless a trusted-proxy list is configured: middleware.ClientIP returns RemoteAddr when loadTrustedProxyCIDRs is empty (internal/middleware/ratelimit.go:451). Where a proxy is configured and trusted, the forwarded chain is walked from the right to the first untrusted hop by lastRealIP, which is what keeps a client-supplied prefix out of the rate-limit bucket key.

requirements.requirement: Verify that the application explicitly ensures that variables are of the correct type and performs strict equality and comparator operations. This is to avoid type juggling or type confusion vulnerabilities caused by the application code making an assumption about a variable type.
requirements.notes: Go is statically typed with no coercion; secret comparisons use constant-time equality.

requirements.requirement: Verify that JavaScript code is written in a way that prevents prototype pollution, for example, by using Set() or Map() instead of object literals.
requirements.notes: Prototype pollution is a defect class of JavaScript objects, and Go objects have no prototype chain, so the requirement addresses a language construct the server-side code does not use. For the browser application it is assessed separately under the declared scope.

requirements.requirement: Verify that the application has defenses against HTTP parameter pollution attacks, particularly if the application framework makes no distinction about the source of request parameters (query string, body parameters, cookies, or header fields).
requirements.notes: Parameters are read through net/url and net/http accessors, which take the first value deterministically, and the request bodies are JSON rather than form-encoded.

requirements.chapter: V16 Security Logging and Error Handling
requirements.requirement: Verify that an inventory exists documenting the logging performed at each layer of the application's technology stack, what events are being logged, log formats, where that logging is stored, how it is used, how access to it is controlled, and for how long logs are kept.
requirements.notes: The 40-constant event catalogue, its storage, retention and access control are documented.

requirements.chapter: V16 Security Logging and Error Handling
requirements.requirement: Verify that each log entry includes necessary metadata (such as when, where, who, what) that would allow for a detailed investigation of the timeline when an event happens.
requirements.notes: When, where, who and what on every entry, asserted through the real logger.

requirements.chapter: V16 Security Logging and Error Handling
requirements.requirement: Verify that time sources for all logging components are synchronized, and that timestamps in security event metadata use UTC or include an explicit time zone offset. UTC is recommended to ensure consistency across distributed systems and to prevent confusion during daylight saving time transitions.
requirements.notes: TIMESTAMPTZ storage and a Go time.Time carrying its location, so the instant is unambiguous.

requirements.chapter: V16 Security Logging and Error Handling
requirements.requirement: Verify that the application only stores or broadcasts logs to the files and services that are documented in the log inventory.
requirements.notes: Audit records go to the audit table only; there is no secondary sink.

requirements.chapter: V16 Security Logging and Error Handling
requirements.requirement: Verify that logs can be read and correlated by the log processor that is in use, preferably by using a common logging format.
requirements.notes: Structured rows with typed columns and a JSON metadata field.

requirements.chapter: V16 Security Logging and Error Handling
requirements.requirement: Verify that when logging sensitive data, the application enforces logging based on the data's protection level. For example, it may not be allowed to log certain data, such as credentials or payment details. Other data, such as session tokens, may only be logged by being hashed or masked, either in full or partially.
requirements.notes: Eleven credential key names scrubbed globally and four user-chosen name keys scrubbed on blob events, recursively, without over-scrubbing other classes.

requirements.chapter: V16 Security Logging and Error Handling
requirements.requirement: Verify that all authentication operations are logged, including successful and unsuccessful attempts. Additional metadata, such as the type of authentication or factors used, should also be collected.
requirements.notes: Success and failure are distinct event types with distinct risk tags.

requirements.chapter: V16 Security Logging and Error Handling
requirements.requirement: Verify that failed authorization attempts are logged. For L3, this must include logging all authorization decisions, including logging when sensitive data is accessed (without logging the sensitive data itself).
requirements.notes: Both halves of the requirement are logged. Failed admin authentication, lockout and the killswitch trip were already recorded; RBACCheck now writes an admin_authz_denied event on a permission denial, so a failed authorization decision reaches the append-only audit log with the admin, the role and the permission it was refused. This closes what was tracked as CR-16. The admin plane is loopback-only behind mutual TLS, so the population of principals a denial can name is small and already identified. The context handoff between the two middlewares — SessionAuth resolves the session to an admin, RBACCheck judges that admin — is asserted end to end through the wired router by TestAdminAuth_TheSessionsAdminIsWhatRBACJudges in tests/attack, which is outside the package this row's tests are resolved in.

requirements.requirement: Reauthentication
requirements.notes: Met. Periodic reauthentication is now enforced on both triggers: at the absolute bound by enforceSessionLifetime and on inactivity by enforceSessionInactivity. Section 2.2.3 says that when the inactivity timeout has passed but the overall one has not, a verifier MAY accept a password or biometric together with the session secret. vault42 does not take that option and the choice is deliberate: middleware.Confirmed, the existing prove-it-again control, is a step-up over a LIVE session and requires a valid access token to reach, and an idle session's access token expired 45 minutes before the inactivity bound fires. The only call that could carry a re-proof is the refresh itself, which is the call being refused. So the family is terminated and the user reauthenticates through Login at full strength, which is stricter than the MAY and consistent with what the absolute bound already does.

Least Privilege

Device Lock
requirements.notes: AC-11 governs the session lock an operating system applies to an unattended endpoint. It addresses a control the endpoint owns; a headless authentication server is not where a device lock is configured or enforced. The server-side analogue, bounding how long an authenticated session may live, is AC-12 and CR-14.

requirements.requirement: Session Termination
requirements.notes: Met, both halves. Explicit termination is complete: RevokeAllForUser and RevokeFamily reach every generation of every family, and each state change that invalidates the credential a session rests on calls one of them. The trigger conditions the control asks for are now two, and both terminate rather than merely refuse -- the absolute age bound and the inactivity bound, each revoking the whole family and recording an audit event naming the trigger (session_lifetime_exceeded, session_inactivity_exceeded). Termination is also visible in the concurrent-session cap: issuance clamps a refresh token's stored expires_at to the inactivity window, so a timed-out family stops being counted by CountActiveFamilies instead of holding a slot for the rest of VAULT_REFRESH_TOKEN_TTL. The mechanism is AuthService.enforceSessionInactivity (internal/service/auth.go:2498), called from the refresh path at internal/service/auth.go:1378 before the presented token is spent. It measures idleness from the presented refresh token's own created_at, which is the instant its family last rotated: a family only advances by rotating, the predecessor row is marked used before the successor is inserted, so the row a client presents is always its family's newest generation. No last_activity_at column was added, because that would be a second copy of a fact the row already carries -- repository.ActiveFamily.LastUsedAt already publishes the same value to the user -- and because stamping activity per request would turn the hottest read path in the service into a write. GetByTokenHash already selects created_at, so the check adds no query and no round trip.

This row was an accepted risk, CR-25, for as long as no issuance path assigned cnf.jkt and the middleware therefore compared a proof against nothing.

Two limits, stated rather than rounded up. Refresh tokens are NOT sender-constrained: the refresh token is an opaque value in a __Host- cookie with no jkt column to bind it to, so its protection remains single-use rotation with family revocation on replay, not proof-of-possession. And no DPoP-Nonce is issued, so a proof's replay window is bounded by its iat freshness check and the one-time jti cache rather than by a server-supplied nonce.
