requirements.requirement: Proof Key for Code Exchange: S256 challenge method
requirements.notes: PKCE with S256. The authorize handler derives the challenge from a 32-byte random verifier through SHA256Base64URL (internal/handler/oauth.go:83); plain is not implemented, so there is no downgrade to refuse.

requirements.requirement: OAuth 2.0: refreshing an access token
requirements.notes: The old refresh token is invalidated before the replacement is created, so an interrupted rotation fails closed. Previously carried as a partial (OAUTH2-TOKEN-001) on the grounds that the ordering was unverified; it is now asserted.

requirements.requirement: TOTP: time-based one-time password algorithm
requirements.notes: HMAC-SHA1 is mandated by the algorithm and is annotated at the import; it is not a free choice of hash. No MD5 exists anywhere in the repository. Test repointed in the register-integrity pass to a case that exercises the clause directly.

requirements.requirement: OpenID Connect: ID token validation
Broken Object Level Authorization
requirements.notes: Met: object reads are keyed by (id, owner), not filtered after lookup. The blob service derives a pseudonym from the caller's authenticated subject and every repository read passes it (internal/service/blob.go:142, GetByIDAndPseudonym), so an object id held by a second authenticated user is a miss rather than a read. The service-document store carries a second ownership axis and asserts it directly: internal/handler/servicedoc.go:105 refuses a token with no client id, and the comment above it explains that the scope check alone is sufficient only by accident. TestAPITop10_API1_2023_ObjectReadsAreScopedToTheCallerNotJustFiltered drives a real cross-user read.

requirements.requirement: Broken Authentication
requirements.notes: Met: every route outside a declared public allowlist passes through an authentication guard, asserted by parsing the router rather than by testing the routes that exist today. Tokens are RS256 only with an algorithm allowlist that rejects none and HMAC, are size-bounded before parsing, and are bound to a device fingerprint. Passwords are Argon2id with a pepper; MFA is on by default.

requirements.requirement: Broken Object Property Level Authorization
requirements.notes: Met: every JSON request body in the HTTP layer is decoded through decodeJSON (internal/handler/response.go:24), which sets DisallowUnknownFields, so a property the API did not offer is a 400 rather than a silent write. On the response side the token carries no sensitive property and the audit projection deliberately omits the fingerprint hash. TestAPITop10_API3_2023_UnknownRequestPropertiesAreRejectedNotIgnored also asserts no handler bypasses the strict decoder, because a strict helper half the package ignores is not a control.

requirements.requirement: Unrestricted Resource Consumption
requirements.notes: Met with three independent ceilings. Per-route rate limits on the flows that cost the most, which matters because Argon2id at 46 MiB makes an unlimited login endpoint a memory-exhaustion primitive and not only a guessing one; http.MaxBytesReader on every write path including the two routes exempted from the global 8 KiB cap; and per-user object-count and stored-byte quotas, which are the only one of the three that bounds slow accumulation.

requirements.requirement: Broken Function Level Authorization
requirements.notes: Met: the admin plane's authorization model is internal/rbac, three strictly hierarchical roles and 30 permission constants hardcoded in Go so SQL injection cannot mint one, and 38 admin endpoints are permission-gated in adminapi.NewRouter. The gate is parsed out of the router rather than sampled, so a new mutating route wired without a permission fails the build. On the user plane, scope enforcement is exact-match rather than prefix.

requirements.requirement: Unrestricted Access to Sensitive Business Flows
requirements.notes: Met for the flows worth abusing in bulk here: account creation, credential guessing and password-reset mail. Each carries its own rate limiter, registration can be switched off entirely for a deployment that provisions its users, and a flagged source address consumes the credential-guessing buckets three times faster, which is the control aimed at the distributed version. The reset flow answers identically whether or not the address exists, so it cannot be used as an enumeration oracle while it is being used as a mail cannon.

requirements.requirement: Server Side Request Forgery
requirements.notes: The inventory divides three ways. Four destinations are compiled-in https literals (SendGrid, the HIBP range API, and the Google, GitHub and Facebook endpoints), two are operator-configured (the SMTP relay and the OIDC issuer), and four are named by the issuer's own discovery document. Only the last four come from data, and they are what this control covers: internal/oauth2/oidc.go:188 holds them to the issuer's domain or the operator's list, and Policy.DialContext (internal/outbound/outbound.go:147) judges the addresses they resolve to. Policy.refuseAddress (internal/outbound/outbound.go:208) refuses link-local unconditionally -- 169.254.0.0/16 and fe80::/10, where cloud instance metadata answers -- and refuses loopback, RFC 1918, IPv6 unique-local and RFC 6598 unless VAULT_OUTBOUND_ALLOW_PRIVATE is set, which defaults on only in the dev profile. Because the check is at dial time, a redirect is judged on the same terms as the endpoint it came from. The chart's NetworkPolicy is the network-layer half and it is no longer the stricter one: charts/vault/templates/networkpolicy.yaml admits egress on 443 to any destination by default (networkPolicy.httpsEgress.enabled: true, cidrs: []), because the shipped policy previously left the HIBP breach check enabled in configuration and unreachable in fact. Narrowing it with httpsEgress.cidrs is available and is a defence in depth, not this row's control. Previously accepted risk CR-17, now retired.

requirements.requirement: Security Misconfiguration
requirements.notes: Met: the production profile refuses to start on an insecure default rather than warning about it, and the security-headers middleware sets HSTS, nosniff, frame-ancestors, Referrer-Policy, Permissions-Policy and the cross-origin isolation headers on every response. The chart renders every values file in CI so a default that stops parsing stops the build. The one configuration gap is CR-27, the two CSP directives V3.4.3 names.

requirements.requirement: Improper Inventory Management
requirements.notes: Met by assertion rather than by habit: every route the server mounts must appear in docs/api.md, and TestAPITop10_API9_2023_EveryMountedRouteAppearsInThePublishedReference checks all 51 of them on every build. An endpoint that ships without an entry in the inventory is the one nobody remembers to retire, which is the whole category. The discovery document at /.well-known/openid-configuration publishes only what is implemented and explains its omissions in a comment.

requirements.requirement: Unsafe Consumption of APIs
requirements.notes: Met: vault42 calls three third parties and bounds each answer before believing it. The OIDC provider's metadata is pinned against the configured issuer; the provider's own email_verified claim is required before a first-time sign-in provisions an account, and linking to an existing account requires both sides to be verified; HIBP is consumed under k-anonymity and its outage is fail-open by design. No outbound client sets InsecureSkipVerify and every tls.Config declares a minimum version.

requirements.requirement: Define security requirements for software development
requirements.notes: Met: the security requirements this software is developed against are this register and docs/security.md, both tracked in the repository and both enforced by tests that run on every build. LICENSE states the terms the software is released under.

requirements.requirement: Identify and document all security requirements for organization-developed software to meet, and maintain the requirements over time
requirements.notes: Met: the requirements this software is held to are ASVS 5.0.0 at L1 and L2, declared in meta.scope and classified row by row in this register, alongside the behavioural specification in docs/spec.md. Maintenance over time is the part usually missing, and here it is mechanical rather than intended: every Met row names a test that runs on each build, so a requirement stops being met the moment the behaviour changes, without anybody re-reading the document.

requirements.requirement: Communicate requirements to all third parties who will provide commercial software components to the organization for reuse by the organization's own software
requirements.notes: Not applicable: this task addresses an acquirer that obtains components through a supplier relationship, and can therefore state requirements to the supplier as a condition of supply. vault42 reuses open-source components published to public registries under their own licences, where the acquirer is one of many downstream consumers and the channel a requirement would travel down runs the other way. The obligation that survives is to check what arrives rather than to specify it in advance, and that is classified under PW.4.1 and PW.4.4.

requirements.requirement: Create new roles and alter responsibilities to encompass the SDLC
requirements.notes: Met: .github/CODEOWNERS names the reviewer for each area, so review has an owner rather than whoever is available. Branch review is required before merge.

requirements.requirement: Provide role-based training for all personnel with responsibilities that contribute to secure development, and periodically review personnel proficiency
requirements.notes: Accepted as CR-39. This task assumes an organization with roles to assign training to and a reviewer to assess proficiency against. vault42 is maintained by one person, so training and the review of it would be the same individual on both sides, which is not a control. Recorded as a risk rather than dismissed as inapplicable: the gap it describes is real, and calling it out of scope would be a claim about vault42's shape standing in for a claim about its practice.

requirements.requirement: Obtain upper management or authorizing official commitment to secure development, and convey that commitment to all with development-related roles and responsibilities
requirements.notes: Accepted as CR-39, for the reason above. The commitment this task asks for is an authority above the developer that can be appealed to when a release is under time pressure, and in a single-maintainer project no such authority exists. What stands in for it is that the gates cannot be waived silently: the required checks are branch-protected and disabling one is a visible repository setting change.

requirements.requirement: Specify which tools are to be included in each toolchain
evidence: .github/workflows/nightly-security.yml#`github.ref` and `github.event_name` all resolve to the CALLER's. A group
requirements.notes: Met: the Go toolchain is pinned to go.mod by every workflow rather than resolved at run time, and each security scanner is installed at an exact version (govulncheck v1.1.4, gosec v2.28.0), so a scan result is attributable to a known tool. Every third-party GitHub Action is pinned to a full commit SHA.

requirements.requirement: Follow recommended security practices to deploy and maintain tools and toolchains
evidence: .github/workflows/nightly-security.yml#false on workflow_call, so no pull request ever scanned an image: a
requirements.notes: Met: .github/dependabot.yml configures automated dependency updates, which is the half that was missing. Detection was already automated -- govulncheck, Trivy over source and Trivy over the shipped image, nightly rather than at release -- but a scanner reports a vulnerable dependency and does not raise the pull request that fixes it. Carried as accepted risk CR-32 for precisely that distinction, and the tripwire written to fail the day either a dependabot or a Renovate configuration appeared is what moved this row. It was replaced on that day by TestSSDF_800_218_DependencyUpdateAutomationIsAutomated, which asserts the configuration exists and covers gomod, npm and github-actions.

requirements.requirement: Configure tools to generate artifacts of their support of secure software development practices
requirements.notes: Met: the tools are configured to leave something behind. CI uploads the coverage profile and the test output as artifacts; the release emits a syft SBOM and a build-provenance attestation per artifact class, plus BuildKit's own provenance and SBOM inside each image index; scripts/coverage.sh keeps the profile at a fixed path rather than in a temporary directory deleted on exit. That last one was a real change of behaviour, not a configuration preference: a run that deletes its profile leaves the generated report as the only record, at package granularity, and destroys the evidence for its own headline figure.

requirements.requirement: Define criteria for software security checks and track throughout the SDLC
requirements.notes: Met: the criteria are numbers a build fails against rather than intentions. Go is measured as 100% of reachable statements, where the denominator is a frozen 51-entry exclusion set in which every entry is confirmed and justified; the .NET SDKs against a floor of 100.00 with no exclusions file at all; the two frontend packages against thresholds declared in their own vite configs. Tracking through the lifecycle is the eighteen-job table in CONTRIBUTING.md, which a test now holds to the workflow: it had drifted three jobs behind, and the drift told a contributor that two gates which had just started running did not.

requirements.requirement: Implement processes, mechanisms, etc. to gather and safeguard the necessary information in support of the criteria
requirements.notes: Met: the coverage profile outlives the run that produced it, which is what makes the criterion in PO.4.1 checkable by somebody else. scripts/cov-gaps.py reads that profile to answer which statements are uncovered and to verify the exclusion set against it, asserting covered + excluded == total, so the set cannot grow without the arithmetic failing. The gate also refuses a profile whose counters were compiled from a different version of a file, which is the failure mode that makes a stale figure look like a passing one.

requirements.requirement: Separate and protect each environment involved in software development
requirements.notes: Met for the environments that build and test the software: every job in every workflow runs on a GitHub-hosted label, so each one is a fresh VM discarded afterwards, and no self-hosted runner is registered. Release builds additionally take no Actions cache, because a cache entry is writable by any run on the default branch and a tag build could otherwise be assembled from layers that never came from the tagged commit. The maintainer's own workstation is a development environment this task also covers, and that half is CR-40.

requirements.requirement: Secure and harden development endpoints to perform development-related tasks
requirements.notes: Accepted as CR-40. The build and test environments are hosted and ephemeral, which PO.5.1 records. The endpoint where code is written is a personal machine outside the repository, so nothing about its configuration can be asserted here or checked by a reader, and an assertion a reader cannot check is exactly what this register exists to avoid.

requirements.requirement: Store all forms of code based on the principle of least privilege
requirements.notes: Met: the release archives are covered by a SHA256SUMS file, and one keyless cosign signature over that file covers every artifact in it because every artifact's digest is inside the file being signed.

requirements.requirement: Make software integrity verification information available to software acquirers
requirements.notes: Met: images are signed keylessly with cosign over their digests, the checksum file carries a detached signature, and the workflow requests the OIDC token those signatures need. A signing step without id-token: write is inert, so the permission is asserted alongside the step.

requirements.requirement: Securely archive the necessary files and supporting data to be retained for each release
requirements.notes: Met: CHANGELOG.md records what changed in each release, the release job publishes the archives and their checksums, and the chart and images are published at the same version.

requirements.requirement: Collect, safeguard, maintain and share provenance data for all components
requirements.notes: Met: BuildKit provenance and an SBOM are produced for each of the three images, and syft SBOMs for the release archives. Stated precisely: provenance: true is BuildKit provenance in mode=min, which is not the same as a signed SLSA build-level attestation, and the register makes no SLSA level claim on the strength of it.

requirements.requirement: Use forms of risk modeling to help assess the security risk for the software
requirements.notes: Met, and in executable form. docs/architecture.md documents the flows that carry a credential, docs/security.md records eighteen accepted risks each arguing its own residual, and tests/attack holds 376 tests that each encode an attack which either used to work or must never work. That last is the difference between a threat model and a threat-model document: removing a mitigation fails the build rather than contradicting a diagram nobody re-reads.

requirements.requirement: Track and maintain the software's security requirements, risks, and design decisions
requirements.notes: Met: every accepted risk carries a rationale, a compensating control, a residual-risk statement, a revisit condition and a named accepting party, and a test rejects an entry missing any of the five. Design decisions that did not become risks are recorded in the changelog, which states what was wrong and what changed rather than what was released. Requirements are the register itself.

requirements.requirement: Where appropriate, build in support for using standardized security features and services
requirements.notes: Met: the security-relevant mechanisms are the standardized ones rather than bespoke equivalents, and the tests check conformance against the specifications rather than against the implementation. OAuth 2.0 with PKCE S256, OpenID Connect discovery, JWT under the RFC 8725 best-current-practice rules, TOTP verified against RFC 6238's own appendix B vectors, WebAuthn, and argon2id for password storage. The IETF and OpenID rows in this register are that verification in detail.

requirements.requirement: Have a qualified person who was not involved with the design, and/or automated processes in the toolchain, review the software design to verify compliance with security requirements and risk information
requirements.notes: Accepted as CR-36. The task offers two routes and vault42 has one of them. The automated half is real and substantial -- eighteen CI jobs, two coverage gates, the compliance suite -- but automation reviews behaviour against requirements that were already written down, and a design review is what catches the requirement nobody thought to write. The independent-person half is structurally unavailable in a single-maintainer project, so this row records the gap rather than claiming the automation closes it.

requirements.requirement: Acquire and maintain well-secured software components from commercial, open-source and other third-party developers
requirements.notes: Met: go mod verify checks every dependency against its recorded hash and go mod tidy -diff fails when the manifest and the imports disagree, both on every pull request that touches Go. The pnpm side is integrity-pinned by a frozen lockfile.

requirements.requirement: Create and maintain well-secured software components in-house following SDLC processes to meet common internal needs
requirements.notes: Met: the in-house components are the packages under internal/, and the SDLC process they follow is the same one applied to everything else -- the reachable-coverage gate, the linter set held against a ratcheting baseline, the attack suite, and the compliance rows that name a test each. The exclusion set is what makes the coverage claim about these components specific rather than aggregate: each of the 51 excluded statements names the file, the line and the reason.

requirements.requirement: Verify that acquired third-party software components comply with the requirements
requirements.notes: Met: go mod verify checks every module against its recorded hash and go mod tidy -diff fails when the manifest and the imports disagree, both on every pull request touching Go; the frontend resolves through a frozen lockfile that pins by integrity. Nightly govulncheck reports at symbol level rather than module level, so a vulnerable package that is present but never called is reported as such instead of as a finding to argue about, and Trivy scans the source, the images and the frontend base separately.

requirements.requirement: Follow all secure coding practices that are appropriate to the development languages and environment
requirements.notes: Met: the standard is .golangci.yml, and it is a standard rather than a preference because a pull request that violates it does not merge. The enabled set is chosen for classes of defect rather than for style -- bodyclose for leaked connections, errorlint for equality comparisons that stop matching once an error is wrapped, nilerr for a nil error returned from the branch that only runs when the error was not nil, sqlclosecheck for unclosed rows. The whole-tree run is held against a baseline that only ratchets down, so a finding in untouched code cannot sit there indefinitely.

requirements.requirement: Use compiler, interpreter, and build tools that offer features to improve executable security
requirements.notes: Met: CGO_ENABLED=0 so the result is a static binary with no dependency on the builder's libc, -trimpath so no absolute build path is recorded, -buildvcs=false and -buildid= so the output does not vary with the state of the tree or the toolchain cache, and a distroless nonroot base with no shell for the binary to land in. The archives are reproducible bit for bit; the images are not, because the Dockerfiles use BuildKit cache mounts, and the register says so rather than letting the stronger claim cover both.

requirements.requirement: Determine which compiler, interpreter, and build tool features should be used and how each should be configured, then implement and use the approved configurations
requirements.notes: Met, and this row is why the task is separate from PW.6.1. vault42 ships the same three programs twice, by two routes: goreleaser compiles the archives and three Dockerfiles compile the images. Through 1.0.2 they did not agree -- the goreleaser builds set -trimpath and -buildvcs=false and the Dockerfiles set neither -- so the published image binary recorded absolute build paths the published archive binary did not, for the same program at the same tag. Nothing caught it because nothing compared them, and both were individually plausible. The named test is that comparison, scoped to the go build invocation so that a flag mentioned only in the comment explaining it does not satisfy the gate.

requirements.requirement: Determine whether code review or automated analysis should be used
requirements.notes: Met: both, and neither is optional. .github/CODEOWNERS assigns human review; the golangci job runs the linters on every pull request.

requirements.requirement: Perform the code review and/or code analysis based on the organization's secure coding standards
evidence: .github/workflows/nightly-security.yml#Cancellation is on for the nightly, which should never queue behind its own
requirements.notes: Met: golangci on every pull request, gosec and Trivy nightly over source and image, govulncheck against the Go vulnerability database. The nightly job fails on HIGH and CRITICAL rather than reporting them.

requirements.requirement: Determine whether executable code testing should be performed to find vulnerabilities not identified by previous reviews, analysis, or testing and, if so, which types
requirements.notes: Met: the decision is recorded as the job table in CONTRIBUTING.md, which names each of the eighteen checks and what it does, and the types chosen are unit, integration under a real database, attack, fuzz over the parsers, and end-to-end. A test holds that table to the workflow in both directions, because the decision is only evidence while it describes what runs -- and it had already drifted three jobs behind, always in the direction of describing fewer checks than happen.

requirements.requirement: Design the software to meet security requirements and mitigate security risks
requirements.notes: Met: the tests/ tree is the executable form of the requirements in this register, and two thirds of the compliance suite asserts properties of the whole tree rather than the behaviour of one function, because the second kind cannot see a defect that arrives with code that does not exist yet. Fuzz targets run in CI over the parsers.

requirements.requirement: Configure software to have secure settings by default
requirements.notes: Met: the production profile refuses to start on an insecure setting rather than warning, the container images are distroless nonroot, and the chart's every values file is rendered in CI so a default that stops parsing stops the build. MFA and HIBP checking are on by default; the embedded frontend and the DPoP surface are off.

requirements.requirement: Implement the default settings, and document each setting for software administrators
requirements.notes: Met: a default install runs as a non-root numeric user on a read-only root filesystem with all capabilities dropped, privilege escalation refused and the RuntimeDefault seccomp profile named, and docs/config.md documents the environment variables, the profile mechanism that fills in what an operator did not set, and the _FILE convention for secrets. The pairing is what this task asks for and what the test checks: a default is only a default while the document an administrator reads agrees with the file the cluster reads.

requirements.requirement: Gather information from software acquirers, users and public sources on potential vulnerabilities
evidence: .github/workflows/nightly-security.yml#false on workflow_call, so no pull request ever scanned an image: a
requirements.notes: Met: govulncheck, Trivy over source and over the shipped image, all nightly rather than only at release, so a vulnerability disclosed after a release is found without one.

requirements.requirement: Review, analyze and/or test the software's code to identify or confirm the presence of previously undetected vulnerabilities
evidence: .github/workflows/nightly-security.yml#Cancellation is on for the nightly, which should never queue behind its own
requirements.notes: Met: gosec nightly for static analysis, plus the tests/attack suite, which is written as an adversary rather than as a user and is run on the same schedule.

requirements.requirement: Have a policy that addresses vulnerability disclosure and remediation
requirements.notes: Met: SECURITY.md states how to report and what to expect afterwards.

requirements.requirement: Analyze each vulnerability to gather sufficient information to plan its remediation
requirements.notes: Met: SECURITY.md names the channel a report arrives by, and this register plus docs/security.md are where the analysis of an accepted residual is written down, with a compensating control, a residual statement and a revisit condition rather than a status.

requirements.requirement: Plan and implement risk responses for vulnerabilities
requirements.notes: Met: SECURITY.md sets out what happens after a valid report -- fixed privately with nothing in the public tracker describing the vulnerability before the fix is out, shipped in a normal release rather than as a patch attached to an email, described in a Security section of the changelog that says what was wrong and what an attacker could do, and raised as an advisory when a deployed instance is affected. The response timeline and the supported-version policy are in the same document, because a plan that does not say when, or for which versions, is not one a reporter can rely on.

requirements.requirement: Analyze identified vulnerabilities to determine their root causes
requirements.notes: Met: each retired risk in this register states what the cause actually was rather than what the symptom looked like, and the changelog does the same for defects that never became risks. The distinction matters in the entries themselves -- the SMTP finding's cause was that net/smtp.SendMail reports success after sending in cleartext, not that TLS was off; the register's own citation drift was caused by line numbers being maintained by hand, not by a wrong line.

requirements.requirement: Analyze the root causes over time to identify patterns, such as a secure coding practice not being followed consistently
requirements.notes: Met: the register's own gates are the output of this analysis, and each was written after the same mistake appeared more than once. Twenty-one rows were classified Not Applicable on a rationale that read like a scope statement and was in fact a false claim about the code, so na_basis became a closed vocabulary that forces the author to say which kind of reason they mean and to prove an absence with a test. Twenty-eight evidence citations had drifted onto a line that no longer said anything, so the relevance gate rejects a citation resolving to a blank line or a closing brace. The pattern, in both cases, was prose asserting something no mechanism checked.

requirements.requirement: Review the software for similar vulnerabilities to eradicate a class of vulnerabilities, and proactively fix them rather than waiting for external reports
requirements.notes: Met: fixing the instance is where this task starts and not where it ends, so every retired risk names the test that keeps its class closed, and a gate resolves that name against the tree. Seven of the twelve already named one by habit; the other five named source lines, which is a citation to a position rather than to a behaviour and stops being true the moment the file moves. The reviews that found these were internal rather than reported: none of the twelve arrived from outside.

requirements.requirement: Review the SDLC process, and update it if appropriate to prevent the root cause recurring
requirements.notes: Met: each class of defect found has left a gate behind rather than a resolution to be careful. Four linter configurations had been driven to zero by hand and run in no workflow, which described a moment rather than a property and had already drifted back for two of the four, so a job now runs them. The .NET SDKs were published to nuget.org and compiled by nothing until the tag, so a required job builds and measures them on every pull request. The image and archive builds disagreed on hardening flags, so a test compares them. In each case the process changed, not the intention.

requirements.requirement: Privileged Containers: privileged pods disable most security mechanisms and must be disallowed
requirements.notes: Met: no chart template sets privileged: true, asserted across every template rather than on the ones that exist today. Scope: every workload the chart deploys, with no exclusions. The bundled PostgreSQL, the honeypot PostgreSQL and Mailpit were excluded by name while they did not meet the profile; all three have since been hardened and the exclusion is gone, which is what TestK8sPSS_Restricted_ThereAreNoDeviationsLeft now asserts, having replaced the exclusion tripwire that fired on the day the last of them was hardened.

requirements.notes: Met: no workload takes a host namespace in a default render. hostPID and hostIPC are set nowhere, and adminGateway.hostNetwork now defaults to false (charts/vault/values.yaml:591); the admin-gateway template only emits hostNetwork when an operator opts in (charts/vault/templates/admin-gateway.yaml:22), and the chart makes that choice explicit rather than silent. This was accepted risk CR-33 while the default was true. Scope: every workload the chart deploys, with no exclusions. requirements.notes: Met: no template mounts a hostPath. The volume types in use are secret, configMap, emptyDir and persistentVolumeClaim, all of which the restricted profile permits. Scope: every workload the chart deploys, with no exclusions. The bundled PostgreSQL, the honeypot PostgreSQL and Mailpit were excluded by name while they did not meet the profile; all three have since been hardened and the exclusion is gone, which is what TestK8sPSS_Restricted_ThereAreNoDeviationsLeft now asserts, having replaced the exclusion tripwire that fired on the day the last of them was hardened.

requirements.requirement: Host Ports: host ports should be disallowed entirely (or restricted to a known allowlist)
requirements.notes: Met: no container declares a hostPort. Ports are exposed through Services. Scope: every workload the chart deploys, with no exclusions. The bundled PostgreSQL, the honeypot PostgreSQL and Mailpit were excluded by name while they did not meet the profile; all three have since been hardened and the exclusion is gone, which is what TestK8sPSS_Restricted_ThereAreNoDeviationsLeft now asserts, having replaced the exclusion tripwire that fired on the day the last of them was hardened.

requirements.requirement: Capabilities: adding capabilities beyond the default set must be disallowed
requirements.notes: Met: no template adds a capability back. The shared container security context drops ALL. Scope: every workload the chart deploys, with no exclusions. The bundled PostgreSQL, the honeypot PostgreSQL and Mailpit were excluded by name while they did not meet the profile; all three have since been hardened and the exclusion is gone, which is what TestK8sPSS_Restricted_ThereAreNoDeviationsLeft now asserts, having replaced the exclusion tripwire that fired on the day the last of them was hardened.

requirements.requirement: Privilege Escalation: privilege escalation to root must be disallowed
requirements.notes: Met: allowPrivilegeEscalation: false on the shared container security context, which four workloads inherit, and inline on the three that declare their own. Without it a setuid binary in the image regains what runAsUser dropped. Scope: every workload the chart deploys, with no exclusions. The bundled PostgreSQL, the honeypot PostgreSQL and Mailpit were excluded by name while they did not meet the profile; all three have since been hardened and the exclusion is gone, which is what TestK8sPSS_Restricted_ThereAreNoDeviationsLeft now asserts, having replaced the exclusion tripwire that fired on the day the last of them was hardened.

requirements.requirement: This check determines whether the project has generated executable (binary) artifacts in the source repository.
requirements.notes: Met, scored 10 on the 2026-08-20 run: no binaries found in the repo. requirements.requirement: This check determines whether a project's default and release branches are protected with GitHub's branch protection or repository rules settings.
requirements.notes:
Met, and scored 3 of 10 on the 2026-08-20 run. Both figures are true and the row says so rather than quoting the first: the requirement asks whether the default and release branches are protected, and they are, but Scorecard's scale rewards tiers this project cannot reach. main was unprotected through 1.0.0 and the check could not read it at all (-1, reported as an internal error). It now requires a pull request, thirteen status checks including the Go and .NET coverage gates, branches up to date before merge, linear history and resolved conversations, and refuses force pushes and deletion. 

The two warnings that hold it at 3 are 'does not require approvers' and 'codeowners review is not required'. Both are the single-maintainer problem recorded as CR-36, not an omission: GitHub does not offer the Approve control on your own pull request, and .github/CODEOWNERS names @42-v, so requiring a code-owner review is requiring the author to approve themselves. 1.0.1 set the approval requirement and the very next pull request could not be merged except by an admin bypass, which skips the thirteen status checks as well as the review. Setting it back would raise this score by turning the CI gate into something waived on every merge, which is the wrong trade and the reason the score is published here instead of chased. 

enforce_admins is off, which also costs a point. That is a live question rather than a settled one: with the approval requirement at zero it no longer protects anything the maintainer needs waived, so enabling it would make the thirteen checks unbypassable by anyone including the maintainer, at the cost of needing the rule visibly disabled to land a hotfix past a broken CI. It is the maintainer's call and is left as it was explicitly chosen. The required checks are the always-run wrapper jobs, not the conditional gates they watch, because branch protection counts a skipped job as green.

requirements.requirement: This check tries to determine if the project runs tests before pull requests are merged.
requirements.notes: Met, scored 10 on the 2026-08-20 run: 13 of 13 merged pull requests were checked by a CI test. The suite that runs on a pull request is the unit, attack, compliance, spec and fuzz set plus the coverage gate; 1.0.1 adds the .NET SDK build and coverage gate, which until then ran only in the release workflow after the tag had been pushed.

requirements.requirement: This check determines whether the project has earned an OpenSSF (formerly CII) Best Practices Badge at the passing, silver, or gold level.
requirements.notes: Accepted as CR-35. Scored 0: no effort to earn a badge detected. The badge requires registering the project at bestpractices.dev and self-certifying against 67 passing-level criteria, which is an account action outside the repository and cannot be performed by a commit. The assessment itself can be, and is: docs/openssf-best-practices.md answers every criterion against the evidence already in the tree and finds all 67 satisfied, with one qualification -- version_tags, which is honest only once v1.0.1 and v1.0.2 exist as tags. So the gap is the registration, not the practice, and the row says which.

requirements.requirement: This check determines whether the project requires human code review before pull requests are merged.
requirements.notes: Accepted as CR-36. Scored 0: 0 of 14 approved changesets. Every change reaches main through a pull request with CI attached, and 1.0.1 adds a branch-protection rule requiring one approving review -- but the project has one maintainer, so the approval it requires is the author's own or none. The rule still earns its place, because it makes an unreviewed merge a deliberate admin bypass rather than the default path, and the score will move as soon as there is a second reviewer. Claiming Met on a rule nobody else can satisfy would be the overclaim this register exists to avoid.

requirements.requirement: This check tries to determine if the project has recent contributors from multiple organizations.
requirements.notes: Accepted as CR-36, the same single-maintainer fact that holds Code-Review at zero. Scored 0: zero contributing organisations. The check measures how many organisations have committed recently, which one maintainer cannot move by writing better code. It was first classified Not Applicable here and that was wrong: the register's vocabulary for inapplicable requirements covers absent capabilities, roles vault42 does not occupy, and components declared out of scope, and this is none of those. It is a real property of the project, measured correctly, that the project has decided to live with.

requirements.requirement: This check tries to determine if the project pins dependencies used during its build and release process. A "pinned dependency" is a dependency that is explicitly set to a specific hash instead of allowing a mutable version or range of versions.
requirements.notes:
Met; scored 9 on the 2026-08-20 run against main, with one finding left. Every action reference across the five workflows is pinned to a 40-character commit SHA and always was: 69 of 69 GitHub-owned actions, 32 of 32 third-party actions, 11 of 11 container images, 2 of 2 go commands, 1 of 1 pip command.

The findings were installs that named an exact version and then trusted whatever bytes the registry returned, which is a version pin and not a supply-chain pin: a republished artifact under the same version, or an account takeover on ruff, yamllint or markdownlint-cli2, executed in CI on every pull request. pip installs under --require-hashes from a pip-compile-generated file carrying a digest for every resolved artifact including the transitive ones, and markdownlint-cli2 is a root devDependency that pnpm-lock.yaml pins by integrity.

The last one was the corepack install in the frontend build stage, which was already fetched by URL and verified against a committed SHA-256 before anything ran it -- so it was pinned harder than most of what the check was passing, and still scored as an unpinned npmCommand, because the check reads the command and not the verification around it. The tarball is now unpacked with tar instead of handed to `npm install -g`, which removes the finding and also removes npm's resolution, tree write and lifecycle scripts from a package whose bytes were already verified. Verified by building the stage: corepack 0.35.0 and pnpm 10.18.0 both resolve inside the image.

requirements.requirement: This check tries to determine if the project cryptographically signs release artifacts.
requirements.notes: Met by the workflow; scored -1 on the 2026-08-20 run, which reports "no releases found" because the check reads the artifacts of published releases and there were none: 1.0.0 was merged without ever being tagged, and 1.0.1 was merged and not tagged after it. The release workflow is where this matters most: eight of its jobs used to inherit contents: write and packages: write from the workflow, including the ones that run the full test and attack suites, which meant arbitrary repository code executing while holding a token that could push to GHCR.

requirements.requirement: This check determines whether the project has open, unfixed vulnerabilities in its own codebase or its dependencies using the OSV service.
requirements.notes: Accepted as CR-37, reduced not closed. Scored 6 on the 2026-08-20 run with four open advisories; 1.0.1 clears three of them. GHSA-hfg8-hc9c-6c3h in moby/go-archive is fixed by 0.3.3, and two more resolve with the testcontainers and x/crypto upgrades. The fourth cannot be fixed: GO-2026-5932 marks golang.org/x/crypto/openpgp unmaintained and unsafe by design with no patched version, and x/crypto is a direct dependency for argon2 and hkdf. Nothing in this tree imports openpgp, and govulncheck confirms it at symbol level on both modules, but OSV reports per-module rather than per-symbol so the finding stands as long as the dependency does.

Branch protection is also account state and is nevertheless classified Met, because a branch rule governs what enters the tree; a webhook delivers events outward and governs nothing here. The check is experimental, requires a maintainer token to run at all, and does not appear in the published result for this repository.

requirements.requirement: The producer MUST select a build platform that is capable of reaching their desired SLSA Build Level.
requirements.notes: Met. Every job in every workflow runs on a GitHub-hosted runner label; the repository has no self-hosted runners registered, which is the way a release quietly comes to be built on somebody's workstation. GitHub Actions provides ephemeral per-job VMs and keyless attestation through Sigstore, which is what Build L2 needs and most of what L3 needs.

requirements.requirement: The producer MUST build their artifact in a consistent manner such that verifiers can form expectations about the build process.
requirements.notes: Met. The release is driven by an annotated vX.Y.Z tag, not by whatever is on main and not by the subject line of a squash commit -- the subject-driven trigger it replaced is what lost 0.8.6 and then 1.0.0, because a release depending on someone editing a merge message is a release skipped the first time they forget. Three guards keep the run and the tag the same thing: the run's ref must be the tag being published, the tagged commit must be an ancestor of main, and VERSION must agree with the tag. A verifier can therefore expect that a given tag names a reviewed commit and the artifacts built from it.

requirements.requirement: The producer MUST distribute provenance to artifact consumers.
requirements.notes: Met, through the package ecosystem as the requirement permits. Image attestations are stored by GitHub against the repository and resolved by digest with `gh attestation verify`; BuildKit provenance and an SBOM travel inside each image, so a consumer who only pulls still gets them; and the release archives carry syft SBOMs alongside a signed SHA256SUMS.

requirements.requirement: The build process MUST generate provenance that unambiguously identifies the output package by cryptographic digest and describes how that package was produced.
requirements.notes: Met for every artifact class a release publishes, which is the part worth checking: the three images by digest, the Helm chart by digest, and the release archives by path. Provenance covering three of four would be provenance a consumer cannot rely on without first working out which one is missing. The format is in-toto SLSA Provenance, which the spec recommends.

requirements.requirement: Consumers MUST be able to validate the authenticity of the provenance attestation. This SHOULD be through a digital signature from a private key accessible only to the build platform component that generated the provenance attestation.
requirements.notes: Met, and keyless, which is stronger here than a key would be: Sigstore issues a short-lived certificate against the workflow's OIDC identity and the signature is logged in Rekor, so what a verifier trusts is the workflow that ran rather than a key somebody has to keep and could lose. No long-lived signing key exists to be stolen from a runner. cosign signs the images and the chart by digest, so a signature cannot be moved to a different artifact, and one signature over SHA256SUMS covers every release archive.

requirements.requirement: The build platform ensured that the build steps ran in an isolated environment, free of unintended external influence. This MUST hold true even between builds within the same tenant project.
requirements.notes: Met by the platform, with the one clause a workflow can break on its own asserted here. GitHub provisions a fresh VM per job and destroys it afterwards, which covers ephemerality and cross-build memory influence; those are GitHub's guarantees and this register does not pretend to test them. The clause a workflow controls is cache poisoning -- the spec asks that a build produce identical output whether or not a cache was used -- and every setup-go step in the release path sets cache: false, so no module cache is carried between runs. No workflow opens a debug or remote-shell service.

requirements.requirement: Provenance MUST be strongly resistant to forgery by tenants. Every field in the provenance MUST be generated or verified by the build platform in a trusted control plane. The user-controlled build steps MUST NOT be able to inject or alter the contents.
requirements.notes: Accepted as CR-38, and it is the single requirement between this project and a clean Build L3. The secret-material half is satisfied outright: no signing key is ever on the runner, because Sigstore issues a short-lived certificate against the workflow identity, so there is nothing for a build step to read. The failing half is the subject. actions/attest-build-provenance takes subject-digest and subject-path as inputs supplied by the job, so a compromised build step could request an attestation over a digest it did not produce -- that field is not generated in a trusted control plane, it is asserted by the tenant. Claiming L3 on the strength of the key half alone would be exactly the rounding-up this register exists to prevent.
